newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-MUSTER BEATS IVANISEVIC, THROUGH TO SEMIFINALS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER BEATS IVANISEVIC, THROUGH TO SEMIFINALS.

text.p: Croatian hardman Goran Ivanisevic saw his grand slam hopes broken once more on Wednesday when he was blasted out of the Australian Open by Austrian clay court king Thomas Muster.
The world number four played like a nervous underdog and made a string of unforced errors as he went down 6-4 6-2 6-3 to lose out on a semifinal berth.
"I had a lot of chances I didn't take," said Ivanisevic. "And if don't take those chances, you're gone."
Ivanisevic has been in the top 10 for the past five years but has never managed to win any of tennis's four major events.
With the retractable roof over centre court closed for the second day -- but because of torrential rain rather than sun -- Muster appeared to relish the indoor hardcourt conditions.
The super-fit Austrian, shedding the tag of mere clay courter, played a much smarter game, serving smoothly and wearing his opponent down from the baseline.
His semifinal opponent will be either world number one Pete Sampras or Spain's 10th seed Albert Costa and Ivanisevic said he could go all the way.
"If he beats Pete, he'll win the tournament pretty easy," Ivanisevic said.
"You have to take your chances," said Muster. "My goal was to reach the quarter-finals and now I'm in the semis."
In the women's draw, Swiss teenager Martina Hingis breezed playfully into the semifinals with a straight sets victory over Romania's Irina Spirlea -- once again making it look easy.

Hingis, seeded number four, made a tentative start, dropping her second service game but immediately broke back and was never troubled again, winning 7-5 6-2 in just 70 minutes. She has yet to drop a set in the tournament.

There was heartbreak for Belgian giant-killer Dominique van Roost, who handed American 14th seed Mary Joe Fernandez her first grand slam semifinal in four years when she retired hurt in the second set because of a pulled abdominal muscle.
Her defeat ended Belgium's best grand slam performance after the defeat of 16th seed Sabine Appelmans on Tuesday.

After a three-day heatwave where courtside temperatures edged over 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit), the Australian Open was again played indoors. A drop in temperature to around 20 degrees (68 Fahrenheit) brought heavy rain, helping to extinguish deadly bushfires around the southern Australian city.
Hingis told reporters she had been hoping for rain.
"I was like a little praying, please," she said. "I have pretty good scores at the indoor tournaments, I have much better control in there, I like that."
Hingis's mother Melanie, who is also her coach, was quoted saying after her daughter's victory at a warm-up event in Sydney that she was not ready to lift a grand slam title.
"She said 'if you want to win that tournament, you have to work for that'," Hingis said. "And that's what I'm trying."

The 16-year-old, who is aiming to become the youngest winner of a grand slam title since tennis was opened to professionals in 1968, clearly enjoyed her match, smiling and joking with her eighth-seeded opponent.
Both players teased each other with cheeky drop shots and Hingis showed none of the petulance she has shown in previous matches when points have gone against her.
"Everyone is complaining...but she has a right to behave the way she does," said Spirlea.
"She can do whatever she likes with the ball. For us, it (her behaviour) looks ironic, but for her it's fine. She's a nice girl, even if she does beat me."

Fernandez, a beaten finalist in Melbourne in 1990 and 1992, was leading 7-5 4-0 when van Roost, visibly pained and close to tears because of a pulled abdominal muscle, forfeited the match after 66 minutes of play.

Van Roost, 23, had been one of the tournament giant-killers, beating number two seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario of Spain in the third round and then 15th seed Chanda Rubin of the United States despite a painful back.
She had been carrying the muscle injury for about a week but the pain finally got too much on Wednesday.
But she had no regrets: "A lot of people think Belgium is French, sometimes you cannot even see the country on the map...I think now they know more about Belgium from the tennis."
